[2026-10-22T13:03:06.804Z] [INFO]         "content": "# agent-commander\n\n[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/agent-commander?label=npm&style=flat)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-commander)\n[![crates.io version](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/agent-commander?label=crates.io&style=flat)](https://crates.io/crates/agent-commander)\n[![JavaScript CI/CD](https://github.com/link-assistant/agent-commander/actions/workflows/rust.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/link-assistant/agent-commander/actions/workflows/rust.yml)\n\nA JavaScript and Rust library to control agents enclosed in CLI commands like Anthropic Claude Code CLI, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode, Qwen Code, Gemini CLI, and @link-assistant/agent.\n\nBuilt on the success of [hive-mind](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind), `agent-commander` provides flexible language bindings and CLI tools for managing agent processes with various isolation levels.\n\nLanguage-specific package documentation:\n\n- [JavaScript package README](js/README.md)\n- [Rust crate README](rust/README.md)\n- [Shared concepts](docs/common-concepts.md)\n- [Hive Mind parity audit and evidence](docs/case-studies/issue-50/README.md)\n- [Dependency integration example](examples/hive-mind-dependency.mjs)\n\n## Features\n\n- **Universal Runtime Support**: Works with Node.js 22 or later, Bun, and Deno\n- **Multiple CLI Agents**:\n  - `claude` - Anthropic Claude Code CLI\n  - `codex` - OpenAI Codex CLI\n  - `opencode` - OpenCode CLI\n  - `qwen` - Qwen Code CLI (Alibaba's AI coding agent)\n  - `gemini` - Gemini CLI (Google's AI coding agent)\n  - `agent` - @link-assistant/agent (OpenCode fork with native permission modes)\n- **Multiple Isolation Modes**:\n  - No isolation (direct execution)\n  - Screen sessions (detached terminal sessions)\n  - Docker containers (full containerization)\n- **JSON Streaming Support**: NDJSON input/output for real-time message processing\n- **Model Mapping**: Automatic mapping of model aliases to full model IDs\n- **CLI & JavaScript Interface**: Use as a library or command-line tool\n- **Graceful Shutdown**: CTRL+C handling with proper cleanup\n- **Dry Run Mode**: Preview commands before execution\n- **Attached/Detached Modes**: Monitor output in real-time or run in background\n- **Read-only Planning Mode**: Enforce native no-shell/no-write restrictions for supported tools\n- **Prompt File Input**: Pipe large prompts through files for stdin-based tools instead of embedding them in shell commands\n\n## Installation\n\n### As a global CLI tool\n\n```bash\nnpm install -g agent-commander\n```\n\n### As a library\n\n```bash\nnpm install agent-commander\n```\n\n### From the GitHub repository\n\n```bash\nnpm install github:link-assistant/agent-commander\n```\n\n### For Deno\n\n```javascript\nimport { agent } from \"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/link-assistant/agent-commander/main/js/src/index.mjs\";\n```\n\n### For Bun\n\n```bash\nbun add agent-commander\n```\n\n## Supported Tools\n\n| Tool       | Description               | JSON Output      | JSON Input       | Read-only Mode                       | Model Aliases                                                   |\n| ---------- | ------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `claude`   | Anthropic Claude Code CLI | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ `--permission-mode plan`          | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`                                       |\n| `codex`    | OpenAI Codex CLI          | ✅               | ❌               | ✅ `--sandbox read-only`             | `gpt-6-sol` (bundled default), `gpt-5.4`, `gpt5`, `o3`, `gpt4o` |\n| `opencode` | OpenCode CLI              | ✅               | ❌               | ✅ `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` deny rules  | `grok`, `gemini`, `sonnet`                                      |\n| `qwen`     | Qwen Code CLI             | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ `--approval-mode plan`            | `qwen3-coder`, `coder`, `gpt-4o`                                |\n| `gemini`   | Gemini CLI                | ✅ (stream-json) | ❌               | ✅ `--approval-mode plan`            | `flash`, `pro`, `lite`                                          |\n| `agent`    | @link-assistant/agent     | ✅               | ✅               | ✅ `--permission-mode readonly/plan` | `nemotron-3-super-free` (default), `grok`, `sonnet`, `haiku`    |\n\n### Claude-specific Features\n\nThe Claude Code CLI supports additional features:\n\n- **Stream JSON format**: Uses `--output-format stream-json` and `--input-format stream-json` for real-time streaming\n- **Permission bypass**: Automatically includes `--dangerously-skip-permissions` by default for unrestricted operation; use read-only mode or `--skip-default-safety-flags` to supply a stricter native policy\n- **Fallback model**: Use `--fallback-model` for automatic fallback when the primary model is overloaded\n- **Session management**: Full support for `--session-id`, `--fork-session`, and `--resume`\n- **System prompt appending**: Use `--append-system-prompt` to add to the default system prompt\n- **Verbose mode**: Enable with `--verbose` for detailed output\n- **User message replay**: Use `--replay-user-messages` for streaming acknowledgment\n\n### Qwen-specific Features\n\nThe [Qwen Code CLI](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code) supports additional features:\n\n- **Stream JSON format**: Uses `--output-format stream-json` for real-time NDJSON streaming\n- **Auto-approval mode**: Use `--yolo` flag for automatic action approval (enabled by default)\n- **Session management**: Support for `--resume <sessionId>` and `--continue` for most recent session\n- **Context options**: Use `--all-files` to include all files, `--include-directories` for specific dirs\n- **Partial messages**: Use `--include-partial-messages` with stream-json for real-time UI updates\n- **Model flexibility**: Supports Qwen3-Coder models plus OpenAI-compatible models via API\n\n### Gemini-specific Features\n\nThe [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) supports additional features:\n\n- **Stream JSON format**: Uses `--output-format stream-json` for real-time NDJSON streaming\n- **Auto-approval mode**: Use `--yolo` flag for automatic action approval (enabled by default)\n- **Sandbox mode**: Use `--sandbox` flag for secure tool execution in isolated environment\n- **Checkpointing**: Use `--checkpointing` to save project snapshots before file modifications\n- **Debug output**: Use `-d` flag for detailed debug output\n- **Model selection**: Use `-m` flag to select model (e.g., `gemini-2.5-flash`, `gemini-2.5-pro`)\n- **Interactive mode**: Use `-i` flag with prompt to start interactive session\n\n### Agent-specific Features\n\nThe [@link-assistant/agent](https://github.com/link-assistant/agent) supports additional features:\n\n- **JSON Input/Output**: Accepts JSON via stdin, outputs JSON event streams (OpenCode-compatible)\n- **Native permission system**: Enforceable `--permission-mode` (`auto` | `plan` | `readonly` | `ask`) plus an OpenCode-compatible `--permission` JSON policy (agent v0.24.0); `--read-only`/`--plan-only` map to it directly\n- **Autonomous by default**: Runs with `--permission-mode auto` (full auto, never asks) unless a read-only/planning restriction is requested\n- **13 built-in tools**: Including websearch, codesearch, batch - all enabled by default\n- **MCP support**: Model Context Protocol for extending functionality with MCP servers\n- **OpenCode compatibility**: 100% compatible with OpenCode's JSON event streaming format\n\n### Read-only Planning Mode\n\nUse `--read-only` or `--plan-only` when the selected agent should inspect and plan without shell execution or file mutation. The command builder maps the request to the safest native restriction available for each supported tool:\n\n- `claude`: `--permission-mode plan`\n- `codex`: `--ask-for-approval never exec --sandbox read-only`\n- `opencode`: `OPENCODE_PERMISSION='{\"edit\":\"deny\",\"bash\":\"deny\",\"task\":\"deny\"}'`\n- `qwen`: `--approval-mode plan`\n- `gemini`: `--approval-mode plan`\n- `agent`: `--permission-mode readonly` for `--read-only`, `--permission-mode plan` for `--plan-only`\n\nMost tools treat `--plan-only` as an alias for `--read-only`. The `agent` tool honors its own distinction: `--read-only` selects the hard `readonly` mode (deny every edit and any non read-only shell command, never asks) while `--plan-only` selects `plan` (deny edits, allow read-only shell, ask before anything else). For fine-grained OpenCode-style policies, pass `agent`'s native `--permission '<json>'` through `--tool-arg`.\n\nIf a tool cannot enforce the requested restrictions, `start-agent` fails before starting the agent.\n\n## CLI Usage\n\n### start-agent\n\nStart an agent with specified configuration:\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Solve the issue\"\n```\n\n#### Options\n\n- `--tool <name>` - CLI tool to use (e.g., 'claude', 'codex', 'opencode', 'qwen', 'gemini', 'agent') [required]\n- `--working-directory <path>` - Working directory for the agent [required]\n- `--prompt <text>` - Prompt for the agent\n- `--prompt-file <path>` - Read prompt input from a file\n- `--system-prompt <text>` - System prompt for the agent\n- `--append-system-prompt <text>` - Append to the default system prompt (Claude only)\n- `--model <name>` - Model to use (e.g., 'sonnet', 'opus', 'grok')\n- `--fallback-model <name>` - Fallback model when default is overloaded (Claude only)\n- `--verbose` - Enable verbose mode (Claude only)\n- `--read-only` - Enforce native read-only/planning mode for supported tools\n- `--plan-only` - Alias for `--read-only` for most tools; the `agent` tool maps it to its softer `--permission-mode plan`\n- `--resume <sessionId>` - Resume a previous session by ID\n- `--session-id <uuid>` - Use a specific session ID (Claude only, must be valid UUID)\n- `--fork-session` - Create new session ID when resuming (Claude only)\n- `--replay-user-messages` - Re-emit user messages on stdout (Claude only, streaming mode)\n- `--tool-executable <path>` - Override the native tool executable for any supported tool\n- `--tool-env <KEY=VALUE>` - Add an environment variable to the native tool process (repeatable)\n- `--tool-arg <arg>` - Append a raw native tool argument after agent-commander's typed arguments (repeatable)\n- `--skip-default-safety-flags` - Suppress default autonomous bypass flags, including Qwen/Gemini `--yolo`, so callers can provide their own permission, sandbox, or approval flags\n- `--isolation <mode>` - Isolation mode: none, screen, docker (default: none)\n- `--screen-name <name>` - Screen session name (required for screen isolation)\n- `--container-name <name>` - Container name (required for docker isolation)\n- `--detached` - Run in detached mode\n- `--dry-run` - Show command without executing\n- `--help, -h` - Show help message\n\n#### Examples\n\n**Basic usage with Claude**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Hello\" --model sonnet\n```\n\n**Using Codex**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool codex --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Fix the bug\" --model gpt5\n```\n\n**Using a prompt file for large prompts**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool codex --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt-file /tmp/agent-prompt.txt --model gpt-5.5\n```\n\n**Using @link-assistant/agent with Grok**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool agent --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Analyze code\" --model grok\n```\n\n**Using Qwen Code**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool qwen --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Review this code\" --model qwen3-coder\n```\n\n**Using Gemini**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool gemini --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Explain this code\" --model flash\n```\n\n**With model fallback (Claude)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt \"Complex task\" --model opus --fallback-model sonnet\n```\n\n**Native tool passthrough**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt-file /tmp/agent-prompt.txt \\\n  --tool-executable /opt/claude-code/bin/claude \\\n  --tool-env MCP_TIMEOUT=10000 \\\n  --skip-default-safety-flags \\\n  --tool-arg --mcp-config --tool-arg /tmp/mcp.json \\\n  --tool-arg --permission-mode --tool-arg default\n```\n\n**Resume a session with fork (Claude)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --resume abc123 --fork-session\n```\n\n**Read-only planning mode**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt \"Return a JSON implementation plan\" --read-only\n```\n\n**Read-only planning mode with screen isolation**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool codex --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt \"Inspect and plan only\" --read-only \\\n  --isolation screen --screen-name planning-agent --detached\n```\n\n**With screen isolation (detached)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --isolation screen --screen-name my-agent --detached\n```\n\n**With docker isolation (attached)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --isolation docker --container-name my-agent\n```\n\n**Dry run**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --dry-run\n```\n\n### stop-agent\n\nStop a detached agent:\n\n```bash\nstop-agent --isolation screen --screen-name my-agent\n```\n\n#### Options\n\n- `--isolation <mode>` - Isolation mode: screen, docker [required]\n- `--screen-name <name>` - Screen session name (required for screen isolation)\n- `--container-name <name>` - Container name (required for docker isolation)\n- `--dry-run` - Show command without executing\n- `--help, -h` - Show help Contributing to agent-commander\n\nThank you for your interest in contributing! This document provides guidelines and instructions for contributing to this project.\n\n## Project Structure\n\nThis is a multi-language project with both JavaScript/TypeScript and Rust implementations:\n\n```\n.\n├── .github/workflows/    # GitHub Actions CI/CD\n├── js/                   # JavaScript/TypeScript implementation\n│   ├── src/              # Source code\n│   ├── test/             # Tests\n│   ├── examples/         # Usage examples\n│   └── .changeset/       # JS changelog fragments\n├── rust/                 # Rust implementation\n│   ├── src/              # Source code\n│   └── changelog.d/      # Rust changelog fragments\n├── scripts/              # Shared and language-specific scripts\n│   ├── js/               # JS-specific scripts\n│   ├── rust/             # Rust-specific scripts\n│   └── shared/           # Shared scripts\n├── docs/                 # Documentation\n├── .pre-commit-config.yaml  # Pre-commit hooks\n├── CONTRIBUTING.md       # This file\n├── LICENSE               # Unlicense (public domain)\n└── README.md             # Project README\n```\n\n## Development Setup\n\n### JavaScript/TypeScript\n\n1. **Install Node.js** (22.x or later required)\n\n2. **Install dependencies**\n\n   ```bash\n   cd js\n   npm install\n   ```\n\n3. **Run quality checks**\n\n   ```bash\n   npm run lint           # Run ESLint\n   npm run format:check   # Check Prettier formatting\n   npm run check:duplication  # Check for code duplication\n   npm test               # Run tests\n   ```\n\n### Rust\n\n1. **Install Rust**\n\n   Install Rust using rustup (if not already installed):\n\n   ```bash\n   curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh\n   ```\n\n2. **Install development tools**\n\n   ```bash\n   rustup component add rustfmt clippy\n   ```\n\n3. **Build the project**\n\n   ```bash\n   cd rust\n   cargo build\n   ```\n\n4. **Run quality checks**\n\n   ```bash\n   # Format code\n   cargo fmt\n\n   # Run Clippy lints\n   cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features\n\n   # Check file sizes\n   node ../scripts/rust/check-file-size.mjs\n\n   # Run all checks together\n   cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features && node ../scripts/rust/check-file-size.mjs\n   ```\n\n5. **Run tests**\n\n   ```bash\n   cargo test --all-features --verbose\n   cargo test --doc --verbose\n   ```\n\n### Pre-commit Hooks (Optional but Recommended)\n\nInstall pre-commit hooks to automatically run quality checks before each commit:\n\n```bash\npip install pre-commit\npre-commit install\n```\n\n## Development Workflow\n\n1. **Create a feature branch**\n\n   ```bash\n   git checkout -b feature/my-feature\n   ```\n\n2. **Make your changes**\n\n   - Write code following the project's style guidelines\n   - Add tests for any new functionality\n   - Update documentation as needed\n\n3. **Add a changelog fragment**\n\n   For JavaScript changes:\n   ```bash\n   # Create a changeset file in js/.changeset/\n   cd js && npx changeset\n   ```\n\n   For Rust changes:\n   ```bash\n   # Create a new file in rust/changelog.d/\n   touch rust/changelog.d/$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_description.md\n   ```\n\n   Edit the file with your changes (see rust/changelog.d/README.md for format).\n\n4. **Commit your changes**\n\n   ```bash\n   git add .\n   git commit -m \"feat: add new feature\"\n   ```\n\n5. **Push and create a Pull Request**\n\n   ```bash\n   git push origin feature/my-feature\n   ```\n\n## Code Style Guidelines\n\n### JavaScript/TypeScript\n\n- ESLint and Prettier for code quality and formatting\n- jscpd for duplicate code detection\n- Follow existing patterns in the codebase\n\n### Rust\n\nThis project uses:\n\n- **rustfmt** for code formatting\n- **Clippy** for linting with pedantic and nursery lints enabled\n- File size limit of 1000 lines per file\n\n#### Code Standards\n\n- Follow Rust idioms and best practices\n- Use documentation comments (`///`) for all public APIs\n- Write tests for all new functionality\n- Keep functions focused and reasonably sized\n- Keep files under 1000 lines\n- Use meaningful variable and function names\n\n## Testing Guidelines\n\n### JavaScript\n\n```bash\ncd js\nnpm test              # Run all tests\nbun test              # Run with Bun\ndeno test --allow-read --allow-run --allow-env --allow-net --allow-sys=osRelease test/**/*.test.mjs  # Run with Deno\n```\n\n### Rust\n\n```bash\ncd rust\ncargo test --all-features --verbose    # Run all tests\ncargo test --doc --verbose             # Run doc tests\ncargo test test_name                   # Run specific test\n```\n\n## Changelog Management\n\nThis project uses fragment-based changelog systems:\n\n### JavaScript (Changesets)\n\nThe JS package uses [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets):\n\n```bash\ncd js\nnpx changeset  # Create a new changeset interactively\n```\n\n### Rust (Changelog Fragments)\n\nThe Rust package uses a custom fragment system similar to [Scriv](https://scriv.readthedocs.io/):\n\n```bash\n# Create a fragment\ntouch rust/changelog.d/$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_description.md\n```\n\nFragment format:\n```markdown\n---\nbump: patch\n---\n\n### Fixed\n- Description of bug fix\n```\n\nSee `rust/changelog.d/README.md` for detailed instructions.\n\n## Pull Request Process\n\n1. Ensure all tests pass locally\n2. Update documentation if needed\n3. Add a changelog fragment for user-facing changes\n4. Ensure the PR description clearly describes the changes\n5. Node.js 22 or later, Bun, and Deno\n- **Multiple CLI Agents**:\n  - `claude` - Anthropic Claude Code CLI\n  - `codex` - OpenAI Codex CLI\n  - `opencode` - OpenCode CLI\n  - `qwen` - Qwen Code CLI (Alibaba's AI coding agent)\n  - `gemini` - Gemini CLI (Google's AI coding agent)\n  - `agent` - @link-assistant/agent (OpenCode fork with native permission modes)\n- **Multiple Isolation Modes**:\n  - No isolation (direct execution)\n  - Screen sessions (detached terminal sessions)\n  - Docker containers (full containerization)\n- **JSON Streaming Support**: NDJSON input/output for real-time message processing\n- **Model Mapping**: Automatic mapping of model aliases to full model IDs\n- **CLI & JavaScript Interface**: Use as a library or command-line tool\n- **Graceful Shutdown**: CTRL+C handling with proper cleanup\n- **Dry Run Mode**: Preview commands before execution\n- **Attached/Detached Modes**: Monitor output in real-time or run in background\n- **Read-only Planning Mode**: Enforce native no-shell/no-write restrictions for supported tools\n- **Prompt File Input**: Pipe large prompts through files for stdin-based tools instead of embedding them in shell commands\n\n## Installation\n\n### As a global CLI tool\n\n```bash\nnpm install -g agent-commander\n```\n\n### As a library\n\n```bash\nnpm install agent-commander\n```\n\n### From the GitHub Claude Code CLI | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ `--permission-mode plan`          | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`                                       |\n| `codex`    | OpenAI Codex CLI          | ✅               | ❌               | ✅ `--sandbox read-only`             | `gpt-6-sol` (bundled default), `gpt-5.4`, `gpt5`, `o3`, `gpt4o` |\n| `opencode` | OpenCode CLI              | ✅               | ❌               | ✅ `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` deny rules  | `grok`, `gemini`, `sonnet`                                      |\n| `qwen`     | Qwen Code CLI             | ✅ (stream-json) | ✅ JSON format**: Uses `--output-format stream-json` and `--input-format stream-json` for real-time streaming\n- **Permission bypass**: Automatically includes `--dangerously-skip-permissions` by default for unrestricted operation; use read-only mode or `--skip-default-safety-flags` to supply a stricter native policy\n- **Fallback model**: Use `--fallback-model` for automatic fallback when the primary model is overloaded\n- **Session management**: Full support for `--session-id`, `--fork-session`, and `--resume`\n- **System prompt appending**: Use `--append-system-prompt` to add to the default system prompt\n- **Verbose mode**: Enable with `--verbose` for detailed output\n- **User message replay**: Use `--replay-user-messages` for streaming acknowledgment\n\n### Qwen-specific Features\n\nThe [Qwen Code CLI](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code) supports additional features:\n\n- **Stream JSON format**: Uses `--output-format stream-json` for real-time NDJSON streaming\n- **Auto-approval mode**: Use `--yolo` flag for automatic action approval (enabled by default)\n- **Session management**: Support for `--resume <sessionId>` and `--continue` for most recent session\n- **Context options**: Use `--all-files` to include all files, `--include-directories` for specific dirs\n- **Partial messages**: Use `--include-partial-messages` with stream-json for real-time UI updates\n- **Model flexibility**: Supports Qwen3-Coder models plus OpenAI-compatible models via API\n\n### Gemini-specific Features\n\nThe [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) supports additional features:\n\n- **Stream JSON format**: Uses `--output-format stream-json` for real-time NDJSON streaming\n- **Auto-approval mode**: Use `--yolo` flag for automatic action approval (enabled by default)\n- **Sandbox mode**: Use `--sandbox` flag for secure tool execution in isolated environment\n- **Checkpointing**: Use `--checkpointing` to save project snapshots before file modifications\n- **Debug output**: Use `-d` flag for detailed debug output\n- **Model selection**: Use `-m` flag to select model (e.g., `gemini-2.5-flash`, `gemini-2.5-pro`)\n- **Interactive mode**: Use `-i` flag with prompt to start interactive session\n\n### Agent-specific Features\n\nThe [@link-assistant/agent](https://github.com/link-assistant/agent) supports additional features:\n\n- **JSON Input/Output**: Accepts JSON via stdin, outputs JSON event streams (OpenCode-compatible)\n- **Native permission system**: Enforceable `--permission-mode` (`auto` | `plan` | `readonly` | `ask`) plus an OpenCode-compatible `--permission` JSON policy (agent v0.24.0); `--read-only`/`--plan-only` map to it directly\n- **Autonomous by default**: Runs with `--permission-mode auto` (full auto, never asks) unless a read-only/planning restriction is requested\n- **13 built-in tools**: Including websearch, codesearch, batch - all enabled by default\n- **MCP support**: Model Context Protocol for extending functionality with MCP servers\n- **OpenCode compatibility**: 100% compatible with OpenCode's JSON event streaming format\n\n### Read-only Planning Mode\n\nUse `--read-only` or `--plan-only` when the selected agent should inspect and plan without shell execution or file mutation. The command builder maps the request to the safest native restriction available for each supported tool:\n\n- `claude`: `--permission-mode plan`\n- `codex`: `--ask-for-approval never exec --sandbox read-only`\n- `opencode`: `OPENCODE_PERMISSION='{\"edit\":\"deny\",\"bash\":\"deny\",\"task\":\"deny\"}'`\n- `qwen`: `--approval-mode plan`\n- `gemini`: `--approval-mode plan`\n- `agent`: `--permission-mode readonly` for `--read-only`, `--permission-mode plan` for `--plan-only`\n\nMost tools treat `--plan-only` as an alias for `--read-only`. The `agent` tool honors its own distinction: `--read-only` selects the hard `readonly` mode (deny every edit and any non read-only shell command, never asks) while `--plan-only` selects `plan` (deny edits, allow read-only shell, ask before anything else). For fine-grained OpenCode-style policies, pass `agent`'s native `--permission '<json>'` through `--tool-arg`.\n\nIf a tool cannot enforce the requested restrictions, `start-agent` fails before starting the agent.\n\n## CLI Usage\n\n### start-agent\n\nStart an agent with specified configuration:\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Solve the issue\"\n```\n\n#### Options\n\n- `--tool <name>` - CLI tool to use (e.g., 'claude', 'codex', 'opencode', 'qwen', 'gemini', 'agent') [required]\n- `--working-directory <path>` - Working directory for the agent [required]\n- `--prompt <text>` - Prompt for the agent\n- `--prompt-file <path>` - Read prompt input from a file\n- `--system-prompt <text>` - System prompt for the agent\n- `--append-system-prompt <text>` - Append to the default system prompt (Claude only)\n- `--model <name>` - Model to use (e.g., 'sonnet', 'opus', 'grok')\n- `--fallback-model <name>` - Fallback model when default is overloaded (Claude only)\n- `--verbose` - Enable verbose mode (Claude only)\n- `--read-only` - Enforce native read-only/planning mode for supported tools\n- `--plan-only` - Alias for `--read-only` for most tools; the `agent` tool maps it to its softer `--permission-mode plan`\n- `--resume <sessionId>` - Resume a previous session by ID\n- `--session-id <uuid>` - Use a specific session ID (Claude only, must be valid UUID)\n- `--fork-session` - Create new session ID when resuming (Claude only)\n- `--replay-user-messages` - Re-emit user messages on stdout (Claude only, streaming mode)\n- `--tool-executable <path>` - Override the native tool executable for any supported tool\n- `--tool-env <KEY=VALUE>` - Add an environment variable to the native tool process (repeatable)\n- `--tool-arg <arg>` - Append a raw native tool argument after agent-commander's typed arguments (repeatable)\n- `--skip-default-safety-flags` - Suppress default autonomous bypass flags, including Qwen/Gemini `--yolo`, so callers can provide their own permission, sandbox, or approval flags\n- `--isolation <mode>` - Isolation mode: none, screen, docker (default: none)\n- `--screen-name <name>` - Screen session name (required for screen isolation)\n- `--container-name <name>` - Container name (required for docker isolation)\n- `--detached` - Run in detached mode\n- `--dry-run` - Show command without executing\n- `--help, -h` - Show help message\n\n#### Examples\n\n**Basic usage with Claude**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Hello\" --model sonnet\n```\n\n**Using Codex**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool codex --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Fix the bug\" --model gpt5\n```\n\n**Using a prompt file for large prompts**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool codex --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt-file /tmp/agent-prompt.txt --model gpt-5.5\n```\n\n**Using @link-assistant/agent with Grok**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool agent --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Analyze code\" --model grok\n```\n\n**Using Qwen Code**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool qwen --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Review this code\" --model qwen3-coder\n```\n\n**Using Gemini**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool gemini --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --prompt \"Explain this code\" --model flash\n```\n\n**With model fallback (Claude)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt \"Complex task\" --model opus --fallback-model sonnet\n```\n\n**Native tool passthrough**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt-file /tmp/agent-prompt.txt \\\n  --tool-executable /opt/claude-code/bin/claude \\\n  --tool-env MCP_TIMEOUT=10000 \\\n  --skip-default-safety-flags \\\n  --tool-arg --mcp-config --tool-arg /tmp/mcp.json \\\n  --tool-arg --permission-mode --tool-arg default\n```\n\n**Resume a session with fork (Claude)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --resume abc123 --fork-session\n```\n\n**Read-only planning mode**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt \"Return a JSON implementation plan\" --read-only\n```\n\n**Read-only planning mode with screen isolation**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool codex --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --prompt \"Inspect and plan only\" --read-only \\\n  --isolation screen --screen-name planning-agent --detached\n```\n\n**With screen isolation (detached)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --isolation screen --screen-name my-agent --detached\n```\n\n**With docker isolation (attached)**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" \\\n  --isolation docker --container-name my-agent\n```\n\n**Dry run**\n\n```bash\nstart-agent --tool claude --working-directory \"/tmp/dir\" --dry-run\n```\n\n### stop-agent\n\nStop a detached agent:\n\n```bash\nstop-agent --isolation screen --screen-name my-agent\n```\n\n#### Options\n\n- `--isolation <mode>` - Isolation mode: screen, docker [required]\n- `--screen-name <name>` - Screen session name (required for screen isolation)\n- `--container-name <name>` - Container name (required for docker isolation)\n- `--dry-run` - Show command without executing\n- `--help, -h` - Show help Contributing to agent-commander\n\nThank you for your interest in contributing! This document provides guidelines and instructions for contributing to this project.\n\n## Project Structure\n\nThis is a multi-language project with both JavaScript/TypeScript and Rust implementations:\n\n```\n.\n├── .github/workflows/    # GitHub Actions CI/CD\n├── js/                   # JavaScript/TypeScript implementation\n│   ├── src/              # Source code\n│   ├── test/             # Tests\n│   ├── examples/         # Usage examples\n│   └── .changeset/       # JS changelog fragments\n├── rust/                 # Rust implementation\n│   ├── src/              # Source code\n│   └── changelog.d/      # Rust changelog fragments\n├── scripts/              # Shared and language-specific scripts\n│   ├── js/               # JS-specific scripts\n│   ├── rust/             # Rust-specific scripts\n│   └── shared/           # Shared scripts\n├── docs/                 # Documentation\n├── .pre-commit-config.yaml  # Pre-commit hooks\n├── CONTRIBUTING.md       # This file\n├── LICENSE               # Unlicense (public domain)\n└── README.md             # Project README\n```\n\n## Development Setup\n\n### JavaScript/TypeScript\n\n1. **Install Node.js** (22.x or later required)\n\n2. **Install dependencies**\n\n   ```bash\n   cd js\n   npm install\n   ```\n\n3. **Run quality checks**\n\n   ```bash\n   npm run lint           # Run ESLint\n   npm run format:check   # Check Prettier formatting\n   npm run check:duplication  # Check for code duplication\n   npm test               # Run tests\n   ```\n\n### Rust\n\n1. **Install Rust**\n\n   Install Rust using rustup (if not already installed):\n\n   ```bash\n   curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh\n   ```\n\n2. **Install development tools**\n\n   ```bash\n   rustup component add rustfmt clippy\n   ```\n\n3. **Build the project**\n\n   ```bash\n   cd rust\n   cargo build\n   ```\n\n4. **Run quality checks**\n\n   ```bash\n   # Format code\n   cargo fmt\n\n   # Run Clippy lints\n   cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features\n\n   # Check file sizes\n   node ../scripts/rust/check-file-size.mjs\n\n   # Run all checks together\n   cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features && node ../scripts/rust/check-file-size.mjs\n   ```\n\n5. **Run tests**\n\n   ```bash\n   cargo test --all-features --verbose\n   cargo test --doc --verbose\n   ```\n\n### Pre-commit Hooks (Optional but Recommended)\n\nInstall pre-commit hooks to automatically run quality checks before each commit:\n\n```bash\npip install pre-commit\npre-commit install\n```\n\n## Development Workflow\n\n1. **Create a feature branch**\n\n   ```bash\n   git checkout -b feature/my-feature\n   ```\n\n2. **Make your changes**\n\n   - Write code following the project's style guidelines\n   - Add tests for any new functionality\n   - Update documentation as needed\n\n3. **Add a changelog fragment**\n\n   For JavaScript changes:\n   ```bash\n   # Create a changeset file in js/.changeset/\n   cd js && npx changeset\n   ```\n\n   For Rust changes:\n   ```bash\n   # Create a new file in rust/changelog.d/\n   touch rust/changelog.d/$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_description.md\n   ```\n\n   Edit the file with your changes (see rust/changelog.d/README.md for format).\n\n4. **Commit your changes**\n\n   ```bash\n   git add .\n   git commit -m \"feat: add new feature\"\n   ```\n\n5. **Push and create a Pull Request**\n\n   ```bash\n   git push origin feature/my-feature\n   ```\n\n## Code Style Guidelines\n\n### JavaScript/TypeScript\n\n- ESLint and Prettier for code quality and formatting\n- jscpd for duplicate code detection\n- Follow existing patterns in the codebase\n\n### Rust\n\nThis project uses:\n\n- **rustfmt** for code formatting\n- **Clippy** for linting with pedantic and nursery lints enabled\n- File size limit of 1000 lines per file\n\n#### Code Standards\n\n- Follow Rust idioms and best practices\n- Use documentation comments (`///`) for all public APIs\n- Write tests for all new functionality\n- Keep functions focused and reasonably sized\n- Keep files under 1000 lines\n- Use meaningful variable and function names\n\n## Testing Guidelines\n\n### JavaScript\n\n```bash\ncd js\nnpm test              # Run all tests\nbun test              # Run with Bun\ndeno test --allow-read --allow-run --allow-env --allow-net --allow-sys=osRelease test/**/*.test.mjs  # Run with Deno\n```\n\n### Rust\n\n```bash\ncd rust\ncargo test --all-features --verbose    # Run all tests\ncargo test --doc --verbose             # Run doc tests\ncargo test test_name                   # Run specific test\n```\n\n## Changelog Management\n\nThis project uses fragment-based changelog systems:\n\n### JavaScript (Changesets)\n\nThe JS package uses [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets):\n\n```bash\ncd js\nnpx changeset  # [2026-10-22T13:03:44.064Z] [INFO]         "content": "# Up.computer\n\nThe self-orchestrating control plane for coding agents.\n\nUp.computer brings the agent CLIs you already use into one free, open-source\ndesktop app. Talk an idea through in a chat and it becomes a task that a\nworker agent picks up in the background, on Codex, Claude Code, Cursor,\nGrok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, Pi, or an agent from the ACP Registry.\nEach agent runs on your own subscription, and every chat stays on your computer.\n\n## Status\n\nBug reports and focused feedback are welcome. Large feature work should start\nwith an issue before a pull request.\n\n## Install\n\nDownload the app from [up.computer/download](https://up.computer/download/) or the\n[latest release](https://github.com/krl-gr/upcomputer/releases/latest). Builds are published for\nmacOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows, and Linux, straight from this repository. The macOS\nbuilds are signed and notarized. The Windows installer is not signed yet, so SmartScreen shows a\nwarning on first launch. Installed apps update themselves from GitHub releases.\n\nUp.computer runs the coding agents you install. Set up any you want to use:\n\n- Codex: connect with ChatGPT in **Settings → Providers**, or install the\n  [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) and run `codex login`.\n- Claude Code: install [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code)\n  and run `claude auth login`.\n- Cursor: sign in from **Settings → Providers → Cursor**, or set `CURSOR_API_KEY`.\n  No Cursor CLI is needed.\n- Grok Build: install the [Grok Build CLI](https://x.ai/cli) and run `grok login`.\n- OpenCode: install [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) and run\n  `opencode auth login`.\n- Antigravity: install it and sign in with Google from its provider settings.\n  No CLI is needed.\n- Pi: install [Pi](https://pi.dev) and run `pi` once to finish its login or API-key setup.\n- Other agents: choose **Add provider** in **Settings → Providers** to add an agent from the\n  [ACP Registry](https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/registry) or a local ACP command.\n\nCodex and Claude are on by default. Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity, and Pi are off by\ndefault; turn them on in **Settings → Providers** when you want to use them.\n\nPackage-manager installs such as Homebrew, winget, and AUR are not an official\ninstall path yet.\n\n## Run From Source\n\nRequirements:\n\n- Vite+ `vp`\n- Node 24.13.1+\n- Git\n- At least one supported coding agent, installed and authenticated\n\nInstall Vite+:\n\n```bash\ncurl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash\n```\n\nInstall dependencies and run the app:\n\n```bash\nvp install\nvp run dev\n```\n\nUseful development commands:\n\n```bash\nvp run dev:web\nvp run dev:server\nvp run dev:desktop\nvp run dev:marketing\n```\n\nSee the [development runbook](./docs/operations/development.md) for worktrees, ports, and test\ndata.\n\n## What It Does\n\n- Run multiple coding agents from one desktop GUI.\n- Keep agent work grouped into project threads instead of scattered terminal\n  sessions.\n- Review changed files and diffs before trusting or shipping a run.\n- Commit, push, publish repositories, and open pull requests from the app.\n- Track work as tasks, let saved task agents pick them up by status and tag,\n  and create tasks on a schedule.\n- Give every agent a managed browser and native desktop observation and control.\n- Work against local projects with the desktop app's built-in backend, and pair a browser or\n  another desktop app with it over your local network or Tailscale.\n\n## Repository Layout\n\n- `apps/desktop`: Electron desktop shell and desktop release integration.\n- `apps/server`: Node.js server that brokers provider sessions and serves the\n  web app.\n- `apps/web`: React/Vite application for the main product UI.\n- `apps/mobile`: React Native client from upstream. Up.computer does not publish it yet.\n- `apps/marketing`: Astro marketing and download site.\n- `packages/contracts`: Shared Effect Schema contracts for provider events,\n  WebSocket protocol, settings, and session types.\n- `packages/shared`: Shared runtime utilities consumed by server and clients.\n- `packages/client-runtime`: Client code shared by web and mobile.\n- `packages/effect-acp` and `packages/effect-codex-app-server`: Agent protocol clients.\n- `packages/ssh` and `packages/tailscale`: Remote-environment support.\n- `packages/tasks-*`: Tasks, task agents, and automations.\n- `packages/computer-use-*`: Browser automation and computer use.\n- `infra/relay`: Connect relay from upstream, not deployed for Up.computer yet.\n- `docs`: User-facing and operational docs.\n\n## Relationship To T3 Code\n\nUp.computer is built as a fork of the open-source T3 Code project:\n\n<https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code>\n\nThis fork keeps the upstream runtime, provider orchestration, contracts,\ndesktop infrastructure, and release plumbing close to upstream while developing\na different product direction, UI, branding, and workflow layer.\n\nInternal identifiers keep their T3 Code names so upstream merges stay cheap and upstream clients\nstay compatible: the `@t3tools/*` package scope, `T3CODE_*` environment variables, the `t3` CLI\nname, and the pairing protocol. The application identity, protocol links, updates, and data\ndirectories use Up.computer names. See [docs/branding.md](./docs/branding.md).\n\n## Contributing\n\nThe project is early and the architecture is still settling. Small, focused bug\nfixes, reliability improvements, performance improvements, and clear docs fixes\nare the easiest contributions to review.\n\nIf you want to make a non-trivial product, UI, or architecture change, open an\nissue first so scope can be discussed before you spend time on a large branch.\n\nRead [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening a pull request.\n\n## Security\n\nPlease do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues. Email\n**support@up.computer** instead.\n\n## License And Brand\n\nThe source code is MIT licensed. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE). Release builds also bundle third-party\ncomponents under their own licenses; the app lists them under **Settings → General → Open source\nlicenses**.\n\nThe MIT license does not grant trademark rights in the Up.computer name, logo,\nor visual identity. You may use the name to refer to this project, but do not\nuse the branding in a way that implies endorsement or an official build unless\nyou have permission.\n\nLicensing, privacy, security, or support questions: **support@up.computer**.\n# T3 Code\n\nT3 Code is a minimal GUI for coding agents. A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients.\n\nYou can think of T3 Code as an open source \"bring-your-own-subscription\" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor.\n\n## What makes T3 Code special?\n\nWe have over 500,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on.\n\n### 1. Open at the core\n\nT3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way.\n\n### 2. Performance without compromise\n\nLots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and \"slop\". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.\n\n### 3. Remote ready\n\nThe architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported.\n\n### 4. Multi-surface\n\nT3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**.\n\n**Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing \"app.t3.codes\" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable.\n\n**Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app.\n\n**Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely.\n\n## A note from Theo\n\nI like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.\n\nChannel both \"measure twice, cut once\" and \"yagni\". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.\n\nThe rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as \"hard rules\", more as \"good defaults\". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here.\n\nOf note: Most T3 Code contributions will come from T3 Code itself, often controlled remotely. This means you should be careful about accessing data, killing dev servers, and other things that may damage the T3 Code instance that the contributor is using.\n\n## A small glossary\n\nWe need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:\n\n- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code.\n- **we, us, and maintainers** mean Theo, Julius and the people building T3 Code. These are who you are talking to now.\n- **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents.\n- **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you.\n- **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode.\n- **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI.\n- **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns.\n- **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory.\n- **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project.\n- **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing.\n- **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory.\n\n## The three ways to hurt yourself\n\n1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc/<pid>/cwd` is your worktree.\n2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. Reading it and copying from it are fine, and a good way to get real test data (see Test data). Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.\n3. **Baking in origins.** Never set `VITE_HTTP_URL` or `VITE_WS_URL` for dev. Dev is single-origin and Vite proxies `/api`, `/ws`, `/oauth`, and `/.well-known`. Setting them bakes localhost into the bundle and silently breaks every remote browser.\n\n## Hit every surface\n\nThe most common defect in this repo is a change that works on the path you tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling frontend work done, walk this list and say which entries applied:\n\n- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the chat view is usually also reachable from Settings, the command palette, and a keybinding. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.\n- **Clients.** Web, desktop (wraps web, adds Electron shell/IPC), and mobile (React Native, separate navigation). Shared logic lives in `packages/client-runtime`\n- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is \"not supported here\".\n- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.\n- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.\n- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.\n- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.\n- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.\n\n## Dev servers\n\n- `vp i` installs. Worktrees get this from the t3.json setup script; if module resolution looks broken, it probably did not run.\n- `vp run dev` starts server and web. In a worktree, state defaults to that worktree's gitignored `.t3`, which deliberately outranks an ambient `T3CODE_HOME` so you cannot land on shared state by accident. An explicit `--home-dir` still wins.\n- Ports derive from the worktree path and are stable across restarts, but read the real ones from the `[dev-runner]` line since occupied ports shift.\n- Sharing over the tailnet is three steps: run `vp run dev --share` in the background, wait for the `pairingUrl:` line in its output, then give that full URL to an unpaired browser. Do not wire up `tailscale serve` by hand, open the URL yourself, or consume the user's pairing link. A browser with the reusable dev cookie can use the bare origin. If a normal one-time token was consumed, mint a fresh one with `node apps/server/src/bin.ts pair`. It carries standard scopes, while the startup URL carries admin scopes needed for Connections settings.\n- To reuse web dev auth across worktrees, configure one fixed `T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN` in the main checkout's gitignored `.env`. The `t3.json` setup links that file into worktrees. Never commit or publish the token or a startup URL. See [Reusable dev credential](docs/operations/development.md#reusable-dev-credential).\n- Stop what you started, by the PID you tracked. See rule 1.\n\n## Test data\n\nAn empty database is a bad test. Seed your worktree's `.t3` with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state:\n\n- Run `vp run migrate-dev-db` with your dev server stopped. It rebuilds `<worktree>/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite` from a read-only snapshot of `~/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite`, the developer's real data. It keeps recent projects and their stopped threads, and drops scheduled tasks, pending work, and auth sessions, so your dev server never runs the developer's agents. Raise `--projects` and `--threads-per-project` for more data.\n- Refresh `statev2.sqlite`, not `state.sqlite`. The server copies the V1 `state.sqlite` only when `statev2.sqlite` is missing.\n- Bring `secrets` and `settings.json` only if the flow under test needs them.\n- Copy in, never symlink. Data flows one way: into your sandbox, never back out.\n\n## Verifying\n\n- Smallest proof that the change works. `vp test run <files>` for the tests you touched, targeted lint and typecheck for the scope you changed.\n- Test meaningful logic or observable behavior. Do not render components to static markup to assert props or attributes, or add tests that merely assert callback wiring or mirror the implementation.\n- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No `vp check`, no `vp run -r test`, no `vp run -r typecheck` unless I ask. CI owns the full suite.\n- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.\n- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong.\n- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.\n\nFor authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is a build step, not a blocker. Run `node scripts/mobile-native-client.ts ensure <ios|android> <device-id>` on the simulator host before starting Metro. It checks the local Expo fingerprint and builds/installs when needed. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.\n\n## Pull requests\n\n- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.\n- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.\n- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.\n- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.\n- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.\n- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.\n- When babysitting: poll checks and comments newer than the last push, verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.\n\n## Documentation\n\nMost code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.\n\n- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.\n- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.\n- Keep a local implementation explanation in a nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.\n- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.\n- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.\n- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.\n- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.\n\n## Plans and work artifacts\n\n- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.\n- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.\n- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.\n\n## How it works\n\nClients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.\n\nArchitecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`\n\n## Where code lives\n\n- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.\n- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.\n- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.\n- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.\n- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.\n- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency.\n\n## The application identity, protocol links, updates, and data\ndirectories use Up.computer names. See [docs/branding.md](./docs/branding.md).\n\n## Contributing\n\nThe project is early and the architecture is still settling. Small, focused bug\nfixes, reliability improvements, performance improvements, and clear docs fixes\nare the easiest contributions to review.\n\nIf you want to make a non-trivial product, UI, or architecture change, open an\nissue first so scope can be discussed before you spend time on a large branch.\n\nRead [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening a pull request.\n\n## Security\n\nPlease do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues. Email\n**support@up.computer** instead.\n\n## License And Brand\n\nThe source code is MIT licensed. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE). Release builds also bundle third-party\ncomponents under their own licenses; the app lists them under **Settings → General → Open source\nlicenses**.\n\nThe MIT license does not grant trademark rights in the Up.computer name, logo,\nor visual identity. You may use the name to refer to this project, but do not\nuse the branding in a way that implies endorsement or an official build unless\nyou have permission.\n\nLicensing, privacy, security, or support questions: **support@up.computer**.\n# T3 Code\n\nT3 Code is a minimal GUI for coding agents. A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients.\n\nYou can think of T3 Code as an open source \"bring-your-own-subscription\" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor.\n\n## What makes T3 Code special?\n\nWe have over 500,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on.\n\n### 1. Open at the core\n\nT3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way.\n\n### 2. Performance without compromise\n\nLots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and \"slop\". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.\n\n### 3. Remote ready\n\nThe architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported.\n\n### 4. Multi-surface\n\nT3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**.\n\n**Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing \"app.t3.codes\" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable.\n\n**Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app.\n\n**Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely.\n\n## A note from Theo\n\nI like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.\n\nChannel both \"measure twice, cut once\" and \"yagni\". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.\n\nThe rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as \"hard rules\", more as \"good defaults\". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here.\n\nOf note: Most T3 Code contributions will come from T3 Code itself, often controlled remotely. This means you should be careful about accessing data, killing dev servers, and other things that may damage the T3 Code instance that the contributor is using.\n\n## A small glossary\n\nWe need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:\n\n- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code.\n- **we, us, and maintainers** mean Theo, Julius and the people building T3 Code. These are who you are talking to now.\n- **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents.\n- **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you.\n- **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode.\n- **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI.\n- **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns.\n- **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory.\n- **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project.\n- **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing.\n- **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory.\n\n## The three ways to hurt yourself\n\n1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc/<pid>/cwd` is your worktree.\n2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. Reading it and copying from it are fine, and a good way to get real test data (see Test data). Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.\n3. **Baking in origins.** Never set `VITE_HTTP_URL` or `VITE_WS_URL` for dev. Dev is single-origin and Vite proxies `/api`, `/ws`, `/oauth`, and `/.well-known`. Setting them bakes localhost into the bundle and silently breaks every remote browser.\n\n## Hit every surface\n\nThe most common defect in this repo is a change that works on the path you tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling frontend work done, walk this list and say which entries applied:\n\n- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the chat view is usually also reachable from Settings, the command palette, and a keybinding. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.\n- **Clients.** Web, desktop (wraps web, adds Electron shell/IPC), and mobile (React Native, separate navigation). Shared logic lives in `packages/client-runtime`\n- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is \"not supported here\".\n- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.\n- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.\n- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.\n- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.\n- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.\n\n## Dev servers\n\n- `vp i` installs. Worktrees get this from the t3.json setup script; if module resolution looks broken, it probably did not run.\n- `vp run dev` starts server and web. In a worktree, state defaults to that worktree's gitignored `.t3`, which deliberately outranks an ambient `T3CODE_HOME` so you cannot land on shared state by accident. An explicit `--home-dir` still wins.\n- Ports derive from the worktree path and are stable across restarts, but read the real ones from the `[dev-runner]` line since occupied ports shift.\n- Sharing over the tailnet is three steps: run `vp run dev --share` in the background, wait for the `pairingUrl:` line in its output, then give that full URL to an unpaired browser. Do not wire up `tailscale serve` by hand, open the URL yourself, or consume the user's pairing link. A browser with the reusable dev cookie can use the bare origin. If a normal one-time token was consumed, mint a fresh one with `node apps/server/src/bin.ts pair`. It carries standard scopes, while the startup URL carries admin scopes needed for Connections settings.\n- To reuse web dev auth across worktrees, configure one fixed `T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN` in the main checkout's gitignored `.env`. The `t3.json` setup links that file into worktrees. Never commit or publish the token or a startup URL. See [Reusable dev credential](docs/operations/development.md#reusable-dev-credential).\n- Stop what you started, by the PID you tracked. See rule 1.\n\n## Test data\n\nAn empty database is a bad test. Seed your worktree's `.t3` with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state:\n\n- Run `vp run migrate-dev-db` with your dev server stopped. It rebuilds `<worktree>/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite` from a read-only snapshot of `~/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite`, the developer's real data. It keeps recent projects and their stopped threads, and drops scheduled tasks, pending work, and auth sessions, so your dev server never runs the developer's agents. Raise `--projects` and `--threads-per-project` for more data.\n- Refresh `statev2.sqlite`, not `state.sqlite`. The server copies the V1 `state.sqlite` only when `statev2.sqlite` is missing.\n- Bring `secrets` and `settings.json` only if the flow under test needs them.\n- Copy in, never symlink. Data flows one way: into your sandbox, never back out.\n\n## Verifying\n\n- Smallest proof that the change works. `vp test run <files>` for the tests you touched, targeted lint and typecheck for the scope you changed.\n- Test meaningful logic or observable behavior. Do not render components to static markup to assert props or attributes, or add tests that merely assert callback wiring or mirror the implementation.\n- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No `vp check`, no `vp run -r test`, no `vp run -r typecheck` unless I ask. CI owns the full suite.\n- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.\n- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong.\n- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.\n\nFor authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is a build step, not a blocker. Run `node scripts/mobile-native-client.ts ensure <ios|android> <device-id>` on the simulator host before starting Metro. It checks the local Expo fingerprint and builds/installs when needed. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.\n\n## Pull requests\n\n- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.\n- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.\n- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.\n- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.\n- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.\n- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.\n- When babysitting: poll checks and comments newer than the last push, verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.\n\n## Documentation\n\nMost code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.\n\n- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.\n- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.\n- Keep a local implementation explanation in a nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.\n- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.\n- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.\n- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.\n- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.\n\n## Plans and work artifacts\n\n- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.\n- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.\n- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.\n\n## How it works\n\nClients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.\n\nArchitecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`\n\n## Where code lives\n\n- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.\n- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.\n- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.\n- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.\n- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.\n- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency.\n\n##
